3178.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse auk (“also, too”), preserved in Norwegian dialects, from Proto-Germanic *auk (“also, too”). In modern Bokmål, au is chiefly a dialectal form corresponding to òg (“also, too”) and også (“also, too”).
The further origin of the Proto-Germanic form is uncertain. It has been analysed as *h₂ew (“away, again”) + *ge (“intensifier”), while *h₂ewg- has also been compared.
Cognate with Icelandic auk, Faroese og, Swedish ock, Danish og, Dutch ook, German auch, and English eke.

1004138.etyen:
From heim + kok. The first part him is a dialectal form of heim (“home”), from Old Norse heima, genitive indefinite plural form of heimr (“realm, region, village, home”), from Proto-Germanic *haimaz (“home, house, village”); ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóymos (“village, home”).
The second part is related to the verb koke (“to boil”), from German Low German koken (“cook”) and late Proto-Germanic *kukōną (“cook”); the latter was borrowed from Latin coquō (“to cook, prepare food”), ultimately from the root *pekʷ- (“to cook, become ripe”).

Borrowed from German Hebraist (“scholar of Hebrew”); compare -ist (“specialist suffix”). Compare Danish hebraist and Swedish hebraist (“Hebraist”).

1004906.etyen:

The first element, samarbeid (“cooperation, collaboration”), is related to samarbeide (“to cooperate, collaborate”), formed with sam- (“together”) and arbeide (“to work”). The second element, evne (“ability, capacity”), is from Old Norse efni (“material; subject; task; condition, opportunity”), and is historically the same word as emne (“subject, topic; material”).
